claim: Drosophila ORC forms a stable, hexameric complex containing subunits Orc1–Orc6.
source: Drosophila ORC forms a stable, hexameric complex containing subunits Orc1–Orc6 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Chesnokov et al., 1999, 2001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and by citations to prior work.

claim: Examination of ORC by EM after negative staining showed a monodisperse population of particles.
source: Examination of ORC by EM after negative staining showed a monodisperse population of particles, with no indication of complex instability at the low-nanomolar concentrations used for sample deposition onto EM grids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The addition of 1 mM ATPγS stabilizes ORC in a better defined conformational state.
source: However, the addition of 1 mM ATPγS revealed hitherto unobserved detailed features of ORC, indicating that ATPγS stabilizes interactions between subunits and traps ORC in a better defined conformational state.
evidence: Supported by comparison of 2D class averages with different nucleotides shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The 3D EM reconstruction of Drosophila ORC was refined to a resolution of 22 Å.
source: The structure was refined by iterative projection-matching to a resolution of 22 Å (as judged by the 0.5 Fourier shell correlation criterion) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Supported by Fourier shell correlation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The AAA+ subunits Orc1–Orc5 comprise the crescent-shaped core of ORC in the order Orc1-Orc4-Orc5-Orc2/Orc3.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that the AAA+-like subunits Orc1–Orc5 comprise the crescent-shaped core of ORC, in the order Orc1-Orc4-Orc5-Orc2/Orc3 (when starting at the lower left of the EM structure) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by subunit localization data shown in Figure 2A and summarized in Figure 2B.

claim: Orc6 is flexibly tethered to ORC through Orc3.
source: These data indicate that Orc6 is flexibly tethered to ORC, likely via an interaction with Orc2, Orc3, or both.
evidence: Inferred from EM class averages showing no difference between ORC with and without Orc6, and from GFP-tagging experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Drosophila Orc6 interacts with Orc3 but not with Orc2.
source: Orc6, on the other hand, interacted only with Orc3 and not with Orc2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The subunit order of the core AAA+ subunits in Drosophila ORC is Orc1-Orc4-Orc5-Orc2-Orc3.
source: Since Orc6 appears to contact the subunit at the upper left end in the EM class averages, the Orc3–Orc6 interaction allowed us to refine the subunit order of the core AAA+ subunits to Orc1-Orc4-Orc5-Orc2-Orc3 for Drosophila ORC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Inferred from the Orc3-Orc6 interaction data combined with EM localization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Orc6 is essential and sufficient for Orc3 binding.
source: Surprisingly, however, we found that the C-terminal domain of Orc6 proved to be both essential and sufficient for Orc3 binding when co-expressed in insect cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A for controls).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Full-length Orc6 binds to ORC1–5 with apparent low-nanomolar affinity (Kd, app = 5.0 ± 0.7 nM).
source: Full-length Orc6 bound to ORC1–5 with apparent low-nanomolar affinity (Kd, app = 5.0 ± 0.7 nM) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy binding data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: C-terminally truncated Orc6 proteins do not bind ORC1–5 up to concentrations of 1 µM ORC1–5.
source: Consistent with the pull-down results, C-terminally truncated Orc6 proteins did not bind ORC1–5 up to concentrations of 1 µM ORC1–5 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy binding data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The C-terminal 71 amino acid residues of Orc6 bind to ORC1–5 with an affinity similar to that of full-length Orc6 (Kd, app = 4.8 ± 0.6 nM).
source: In contrast, the C-terminal 71 amino acid residues of Orc6 bound to ORC1–5 with an affinity similar to that of full-length Orc6 (Kd, app = 4.8 ± 0.6 nM).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy binding data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Orc3 contains an additional domain inserted between its AAA+-like and winged-helix domains that is not found in archaeal homologs.
source: In comparing Orc3 protein sequences from various eukaryotes with archaeal Orc1/Cdc6 proteins, we noticed that Orc3 contains an additional domain inserted between its AAA+-like and winged-helix domains that is not found in archaeal homologs (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and structural mapping shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Orc3 insertion is conserved across eukaryotic Orc3 orthologs and varies in length from 70 amino acids in S. cerevisiae to 190 amino acids in Drosophila.
source: This insertion is conserved across eukaryotic Orc3 orthologs, varies in length from 70 amino acids in S. cerevisiae to 190 amino acids in Drosophila, and is not found in Orc1, Orc2, Orc4, or Orc5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Orc3 insertion is sufficient for Orc6 binding.
source: The Orc3 insertion was able to interact with both full-length Orc6 and all N-terminal Orc6 truncations (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Truncating the C-terminus of Orc6 abolishes the interaction with the Orc3 insertion.
source: Conversely, truncating the C-terminus of Orc6 abolished the interaction with the Orc3 insertion.
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Orc3 insertion does not interact with Orc2.
source: Moreover, whereas full-length Orc3 was able to interact with Orc2 in addition to Orc6, the Orc3 insertion was unable to do so, suggesting the Orc2–Orc3 interaction is mediated through the two subunits' AAA+-like and/or winged-helix domains (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The tyrosine mutated in human Orc6 in Meier-Gorlin syndrome is located in a highly conserved, predicted helical element in the C-terminal domain.
source: Intriguingly, the MGS mutation in human Orc6 is a missense alteration that maps to the protein's C-terminal domain, changing a tyrosine at position 232 to serine. The tyrosine is located in a highly conserved, predicted helical element, and is itself highly conserved among eukaryotic Orc6 orthologs, including budding yeast (Figure 6A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and sequence logo shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Drosophila Orc6 Y225S mutation (corresponding to the human MGS mutation) drastically reduces binding to Orc3.
source: When co-expressed in insect cells with MBP–Orc3, drastically reduced levels of Orc6-Y225S and no Orc6-W228A/K229A were pulled-down (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Neither Drosophila Orc6-Y225S nor Orc6-W228A/K229A bind to ORC1–5 in pull-down experiments.
source: Neither Orc6-Y225S nor Orc6-W228A/K229A bound to ORC1–5 in pull-down experiments (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Drosophila Orc6-W228A/K229A shows no binding to ORC1–5 in fluorescence anisotropy experiments.
source: Orc6-W228A/K229A showed no binding to ORC1–5 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Drosophila Orc6-Y225S binds weakly to ORC1–5 with at least 100-fold reduced affinity compared to wild type Orc6.
source: Orc6-Y225S was able to bind weakly to Orc1–5; however, the affinity was reduced at least 100-fold compared to wild type Orc6, and similar results were obtained for the MGS-like mutant when only the C-terminal domain of Orc6 was used in binding experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GFP–Orc6 transgenes containing mutations in the C-terminus are unable to rescue an orc6-null allele in flies.
source: In flies, the Orc6 C-terminus is essential for viability, as GFP–Orc6 transgenes containing mutations in the C-terminus are (in contrast to wild type GFP–Orc6) unable to rescue an orc6-null allele (Balasov et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Balasov et al., 2009).

claim: Mutations in the conserved C-terminus of Orc6 result in reduced ORC hexamer formation in vivo.
source: In contrast, the amounts of GFP–Orc6 mutants that were immunoprecipitated were greatly reduced compared to wild type GFP–Orc6, both in Western blots and when GFP absorbance was measured directly (Figure 7A,B). Thus, mutations in the conserved C-terminus of Orc6 result in a reduction of ORC hexamer formed both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A and quantification shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Chromatin association of Mcm4 is reduced in orc6-null fly larvae expressing Orc6 mutants.
source: After salt extraction of larval brain extracts, the amount of Mcm4 in the pellet fraction was greatly reduced when mutant transgenes were expressed as the sole source of Orc6 (orc635/orc635) compared to larval brains expressing the wild-type GFP–Orc6 transgenes (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Conserved C-terminal residues of Orc6 are required for hexameric ORC formation and for MCM loading onto chromatin.
source: Thus, conserved C-terminal residues of Orc6 are not only required for hexameric ORC formation but also for MCM loading onto chromatin, explaining the reduced DNA synthesis previously observed in mutant flies (Balasov et al., 2009).
evidence: Inferred from the chromatin association data in Figure 7C and cited prior work (Balasov et al., 2009).

claim: Wild-type human Orc6, but not MGS mutant (Y232S) Orc6, binds to human ORC1–5 in vitro.
source: Although weaker than seen for Drosophila, we nonetheless clearly observed an interaction between wild-type Orc6 and human ORC1–5, particularly when an excess of Orc6 was used (Figure 8A). In contrast, human Orc6 containing the MGS mutation (Orc6-Y232S) did not bind appreciably to ORC1–5 (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Human Orc6 containing the MGS mutation does not co-purify with human ORC1–5 when co-expressed in insect cells.
source: Similar results were obtained when human ORC subunits were co-expressed in insect cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Human Orc6 interacts with Orc3.
source: As seen here with the Drosophila protein, human Orc6 has been reported to interact with Orc3 (Figure 8C) (Vashee et al., 2001; Siddiqui and Stillman, 2007).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 8C and citations to prior work.

claim: Human Orc6 containing the MGS mutation cannot bind Orc3 in either the absence or presence of Orc2.
source: Importantly, human Orc6 containing the MGS mutation could not bind Orc3 in either the absence or presence of Orc2 (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The amino acid mutated in MGS patients is critical for formation of a stable hexameric initiator complex.
source: These data indicate that the Orc6 C-terminus is functionally conserved in metazoans, and that the amino acid mutated in MGS patients is critical for formation of a stable hexameric initiator complex.
evidence: Inferred from the binding data for human and Drosophila Orc6 MGS mutants shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Significant homology exists between metazoan, S. pombe, and S. cerevisiae Orc6.
source: However, in the course of analyzing our sequence alignments of Orc6, we noticed that significant homology actually exists between metazoan, S. pombe, and S. cerevisiae Orc6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The homology between metazoan and S. cerevisiae Orc6 includes both the TFIIB repeat domains and the conserved helix in the Orc6 C-terminal domain that harbors the MGS mutation.
source: This homology includes both the TFIIB repeat domains and the conserved helix in the Orc6 C-terminal domain that harbors the MGS mutation, indicating that all of the functional domains present in metazoan Orc6 are conserved in budding yeast Orc6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Budding yeast Orc6 contains an insertion of ∼100–200 amino acids between the two TFIIB-like helical domains.
source: However, in contrast to S. pombe and metazoan Orc6, budding yeast Orc6—as well as related Saccharomycotina (Candida albicans) and Pezizomycotina (Aspergillus fumigatus and Neurospora crassa)—contain an insertion of ∼100–200 amino acids between the two TFIIB-like helical domains, an addition that may have complicated former analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: S. cerevisiae Orc6 binds to Orc3.
source: In pull-down experiments from insect cell lysate co-expressing pairwise combinations of budding yeast Orc2, Orc3, and Orc6, we observed a clear interaction between Orc2 and Orc3, and between Orc3 and Orc6 (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The MGS-like mutation (Y418S) in S. cerevisiae Orc6 abolishes the interaction with Orc3.
source: Strikingly, the MGS-like mutation in S. cerevisiae Orc6 abolished the interaction with Orc3 (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The MGS-like mutation in S. cerevisiae Orc6 is not sufficient to prevent Orc6 binding to the Orc2–Orc3 subcomplex or to ORC1–5.
source: However, in contrast to what we observed with Drosophila and human proteins, the MGS-like mutation was not sufficient to prevent Orc6 binding to the Orc2–Orc3 subcomplex or to ORC1–5 (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 9C and 9D.

claim: S. cerevisiae Orc6 is cooperatively recruited into ORC through interaction with both Orc2 and Orc3.
source: Because Orc6 has been previously reported to interact with Orc2 (Sun et al., 2012), our result suggests that S. cerevisiae Orc6 is cooperatively recruited into ORC through interaction with both Orc2 and Orc3.
evidence: Inferred from the pull-down data in Figure 9C and 9D, combined with citation to prior work (Sun et al., 2012).

claim: Orc6 was still recruited into ORC lacking the Orc2 subunit, albeit at reduced levels, whereas Orc6 recruitment was completely lost in the absence of Orc3.
source: In agreement with this interpretation, Orc6 was still recruited into ORC lacking the Orc2 subunit, albeit at reduced levels, whereas Orc6 recruitment was completely lost in the absence of Orc3 (omission of Orc3 further led to concomitant loss of Orc2) (Figure 9E).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: An MGS-like mutation in yeast Orc6 supports yeast growth, whereas premature stop codons that result in C-terminally truncated Orc6 proteins do not.
source: Consistent with our interpretation, an MGS-like mutation in yeast Orc6 supports yeast growth, whereas premature stop codons that result in C-terminally truncated Orc6 proteins do not (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by yeast complementation assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recruitment of Orc6 into ORC across multiple species is aided by the interaction of its C-terminus with a novel domain that resides between the AAA+-like and winged-helix domains of Orc3.
source: Consistent with this notion, we find that recruitment of Orc6 into ORC across multiple species is aided by the interaction of its C-terminus with a novel domain that resides between the AAA+-like and winged-helix domains of Orc3.
evidence: Supported by pull-down data shown in Figures 4, 5, 8, and 9, and by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A mutation found in patients with Meier-Gorlin syndrome maps to a highly-conserved C-terminal segment in Orc6.
source: Strikingly, a mutation found in patients with Meier-Gorlin syndrome maps to a highly-conserved C-terminal segment in Orc6, destabilizing the interaction of Drosophila and human Orc6 with both Orc3 alone and with the core Orc1–5 subcomplex.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6A, and by binding data in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Orc6 transgenes containing mutations in the conserved C-terminal tail fail to incorporate into DmORC in vivo.
source: Orc6 transgenes containing mutations in the conserved C-terminal tail fail to incorporate into DmORC in vivo, and do not complement an orc6-null allele when introduced into flies.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7A and 7B, and by citation to prior work (Balasov et al., 2009).

claim: The MGS mutation in Orc6 directly affects the integrity of ORC.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the MGS mutation in Orc6 directly affects the integrity of ORC, and indicate that destabilization of ORC contributes to the pathogenesis of Meier-Gorlin syndrome caused by mutations in Orc6, ultimately interfering with pre-RC assembly and origin licensing.
evidence: Inferred from the combined biochemical and in vivo data showing reduced ORC formation and MCM loading with MGS mutant Orc6.

claim: The AAA+ subunit order determined for DmORC agrees with that published for ScORC.
source: Moreover, the AAA+ subunit order determined here for DmORC—Orc1-Orc4-Orc5-Orc2–Orc3—agrees with that published for ScORC (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of subunit localization data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Drosophila Orc6 is flexibly tethered to ORC through Orc3 and is invisible in the EM 3D structure.
source: One notable difference we do observe between yeast ORC and DmORC is that Drosophila Orc6 is flexibly tethered to ORC through Orc3 and is hence invisible in the EM 3D structure (Figures 3A and 10B).
evidence: Supported by EM data shown in Figure 3A and schematic in Figure 10B.

claim: S. cerevisiae Orc6 has been reported to contribute more significantly to EM density of yeast ORC.
source: By comparison, S. cerevisiae Orc6 has been reported to contribute more significantly to EM density of yeast ORC (Chen et al., 2008) and has been reported to bind to Orc2 and not Orc3 (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The more stable conformation seen for budding yeast Orc6 may be due to the existence of binding sites for the subunit on both Orc2 and Orc3 within ORC1–5.
source: Our pull-down data suggest that the more stable conformation seen for budding yeast Orc6 may be due to the existence of binding sites for the subunit on both Orc2 and Orc3 within ORC1–5, as opposed to just Orc3 in the Drosophila complex (Figure 9).
evidence: Inferred from pull-down data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The C-terminal domain of metazoan Orc6 has been thought to be mainly important for non-replicative functions of Orc6 in cytokinesis and daughter cell abscission.
source: The C-terminal domain of metazoan Orc6 has been thought to be mainly important for non-replicative functions of Orc6 in cytokinesis and daughter cell abscission, and in the case of Drosophila Orc6, the C-terminal domain also has been shown to interact with the septin Pnut (Prasanth et al., 2002; Chesnokov et al., 2003; Bernal and Venkitaraman, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Orc6 is essential for Orc3 binding when co-expressed in insect cells.
source: Surprisingly, however, we found that the C-terminal domain of Orc6 proved to be both essential and sufficient for Orc3 binding when co-expressed in insect cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A for controls).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The necessity of the C-terminal domain for Orc6 binding was observed when all ORC subunits were co-expressed in insect cells.
source: The necessity of the C-terminal domain was not limited to binary protein interactions, but was also observed either when all ORC subunits were co-expressed in insect cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The necessity of the C-terminal domain for Orc6 binding was observed when purified full-length or C-terminal truncated Orc6 proteins were mixed with ORC1–5 in vitro.
source: or when purified full-length or C-terminal truncated Orc6 proteins were mixed with ORC1–5 in vitro and subjected to pull-down assays (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Orc6 is required for ORC function and MCM2–7 loading in vivo.
source: Unexpectedly, a mutation in the Orc6 C-terminus linked to Meier-Gorlin syndrome, a dwarfism disorder, impedes proper recruitment of Orc6 into ORC; biochemical studies reveal that this region of Orc6 associates with a previously uncharacterized domain of Orc3 and is required for ORC function and MCM2–7 loading in vivo.
evidence: Supported by biochemical data in Figures 4-6 and in vivo data in Figure 7.

claim: Meier-Gorlin syndrome mutations in Orc6 impair the formation of ORC hexamers.
source: Together, our results suggest that Meier-Gorlin syndrome mutations in Orc6 impair the formation of ORC hexamers, interfering with appropriate ORC functions.
evidence: Inferred from the combined biochemical and in vivo data showing reduced ORC formation with MGS mutant Orc6.

claim: ORC is a heterohexameric protein complex containing the subunits Orc1–Orc6.
source: ORC is a heterohexameric protein complex containing the subunits Orc1–Orc6 (Bell and Stillman, 1992; Gavin et al., 1995; Gossen et al., 1995; Rowles et al., 1996; Moon et al., 1999; Vashee et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Orc1–Orc5 subunits all contain AAA+ or AAA+-like domains.
source: The Orc1–Orc5 subunits all contain AAA+ (ATPases associated with a variety of cellular activities) or AAA+-like domains (Neuwald et al., 1999; Iyer et al., 2004; Speck et al., 2005; Clarey et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A subset of ORC subunits use ATP binding and hydrolysis to support replicative helicase loading, DNA replication, and cell viability.
source: a subset of which use ATP binding and hydrolysis to support replicative helicase loading, DNA replication, and cell viability (Chesnokov et al., 2001; Bowers et al., 2004; Giordano-Coltart et al., 2005; Randell et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding the pre-RC components Orc1, Orc4, Orc6, Cdc6, and Cdt1 have been linked to Meier-Gorlin syndrome.
source: Recently, mutations in genes encoding the pre-RC components Orc1, Orc4, Orc6, Cdc6, and Cdt1 have been linked to Meier-Gorlin syndrome (MGS), a rare genetic disorder characterized by primordial dwarfism, small ears and aplastic or hypoplastic patella (Guernsey et al., 2011; Bicknell et al., 2011a, b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It has been suggested that the clinical phenotype of Meier-Gorlin syndrome is caused by defects in DNA replication initiation.
source: Based on the fact that MGS mutations cluster in pre-RC components, it has been suggested that the clinical phenotype is caused by defects in DNA replication initiation (Guernsey et al., 2011; Bicknell et al., 2011a, b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and inference from mutation clustering.

claim: Cells derived from MGS patients with mutations in Orc1 show reduced recruitment of ORC subunits and replicative helicase components to chromatin.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, cells derived from MGS patients with mutations in Orc1 show reduced recruitment of ORC subunits and replicative helicase components to chromatin, and are compromised in their ability to replicate plasmid DNA (Bicknell et al., 2011b)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recent work has shown a link between origin licensing factors and non-replicative cellular processes, such as centrosome duplication and cilia formation, in MGS patient cells.
source: recent work has also shown a link between origin licensing factors and non-replicative cellular processes, such as centrosome duplication and cilia formation, in MGS patient cells and in cells depleted of licensing proteins (Hossain and Stillman, 2012; Stiff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most MGS mutations in Orc1 lie in the N-terminal domain and have been implicated in interfering with Orc1's Cyclin E-CDK2 inhibitory function of centrosome duplication.
source: Most MGS mutations in Orc1 lie in the N-terminal domain, which is not part of the central core of ORC, and have been implicated interfering with Orc1's Cyclin E-CDK2 inhibitory function of centrosome duplication (Hossain and Stillman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Orc6 is poorly conserved between budding yeast and metazoans, both in sequence and in aspects of its function.
source: Orc6 is particularly enigmatic in this regard: unlike Orc1–Orc5, Orc6 is poorly conserved between budding yeast and metazoans, both in sequence and in aspects of its function (Lee and Bell, 1997; Chesnokov et al., 2001; Prasanth et al., 2002; Chesnokov et al., 2003; Semple et al., 2006; Balasov et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2007; Duncker et al., 2009; Bernal and Venkitaraman, 2011; Chen and Bell, 2011; Liu et al., 2011; Takara and Bell, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Using EM, apo-DmORC is conformationally heterogeneous.
source: Using EM we find that apo-DmORC is conformationally heterogeneous
evidence: Supported by 2D class averages shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The non-hydrolysable nucleotide analog ATPγS locks DmORC in a specific conformation that permitted the determination of its 3D structure to 22 Å resolution.
source: but that the non-hydrolysable nucleotide analog ATPγS locks the complex in a specific conformation that permitted the determination of its 3D structure to 22 Å resolution.
evidence: Supported by 2D class averages in Figure 1B and 3D reconstruction in Figure 1C with resolution determination in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Sequence analyses show that the similarity between yeast and metazoan ORC extends to the domain structure of Orc6.
source: Interestingly, sequence analyses show that this similarity extends to the domain structure of Orc6, suggesting analogous functions for Orc6 from yeast and metazoans.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Destabilization of ORC contributes to the pathogenesis of Meier-Gorlin syndrome caused by mutations in Orc6.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the MGS mutation in Orc6 directly affects the integrity of ORC, and indicate that destabilization of ORC contributes to the pathogenesis of Meier-Gorlin syndrome caused by mutations in Orc6, ultimately interfering with pre-RC assembly and origin licensing.
evidence: Inferred from the combined biochemical and in vivo data showing reduced ORC formation and MCM loading with MGS mutant Orc6.
